tools-and-permissions.summary: Claude Code, not the model, enforces what an agent may do. Every tool call passes through a fixed chain (hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, then your canUseTool callback), and a call approved at any step never reaches the later ones. Know the six modes, the rule syntax for Bash, Read/Edit, WebFetch and MCP, what no mode will auto-approve, and where the OS sandbox takes over from text-matching rules.
points: Evaluation order in the SDK: `PreToolUse` hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, `canUseTool`. A hook can deny outright, but its `allow` does not skip deny or ask rules. Deny rules block even in `bypassPermissions`; ask rules send the call to the callback even in `bypassPermissions`.

Modes (`PermissionMode`): `default` (unresolved calls go to `canUseTool`), `acceptEdits` (file edits plus `mkdir`/`touch`/`rm`/`rmdir`/`mv`/`cp`/`sed` inside the working directories), `plan` (edits never auto-approved, even with an allow rule or hook allow), `dontAsk` (anything that would prompt is denied, callback skipped), `bypassPermissions` (approves everything that reaches the mode step), `auto` (a classifier reviews shell commands, network requests and similar actions).

Set the mode with `permissionMode` / `permission_mode`, change it mid-session with `setPermissionMode()` / `set_permission_mode()`. TypeScript requires `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true` for bypass. In auto mode, switching to an unsupported model drops the session to `default` (a `system` status message), and switching back needs an explicit `setPermissionMode('auto')`.

`allowedTools` / `allowed_tools` adds allow rules; it is not a whitelist. Unlisted tools still exist and fall through to the mode, so `allowed_tools=['Read']` plus `bypassPermissions` still runs Bash. Restrict with `disallowedTools` or the `tools` option. The locked-down pattern is `allowedTools` + `permissionMode: 'dontAsk'`.

Deny rules: a bare name such as `Bash` (or a glob like `*` or `mcp__*`) removes the tool from the request; a scoped rule such as `Bash(rm *)` keeps the tool and blocks matching calls in every mode. Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow; specificity never lets an allow carve an exception out of a deny.

Bash rule syntax: `*` matches any text including spaces; a trailing ` *` that is the only wildcard also matches the bare command (`Bash(ls *)` matches `ls` but not `lsof`; `Bash(ls*)` matches `lsof`); `:*` at the end equals ` *`. Allow rules must match every subcommand of `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|` chains, while deny and ask rules apply when any subcommand matches. Wrappers like `timeout`, `nice`, `nohup` are stripped before matching.

Read/Edit rules use gitignore patterns with four anchors: `//path` absolute, `~/path` home, `/path` relative to the settings source (project root for project settings, `~/.claude` for user settings), `path` relative to the current directory. `Edit(path)` governs Write and NotebookEdit too; `Write(path)` and `Glob(path)` rules never match. A Read deny also blocks Edit/Write on that path.

WebFetch rules use `domain:` (`WebFetch(domain:*.example.com)` covers subdomains but not the apex). MCP: `mcp__server__tool`, or `mcp__server__*`; allow globs need a literal `mcp__<server>__` prefix, so `mcp__*` or `*` in an allow list is ignored. `Agent(Explore)` style rules control subagents.

`canUseTool(toolName, input, options)` returns `{ behavior: 'allow', updatedInput?, updatedPermissions? }` or `{ behavior: 'deny', message, interrupt? }` (Python `PermissionResultAllow` / `PermissionResultDeny`). It fires only for calls nothing earlier resolved, can stay pending indefinitely, and `suggestions` can be echoed back as `updatedPermissions` (a `localSettings` destination persists to `.claude/settings.local.json`). Python rejects `can_use_tool` together with `permission_prompt_tool_name`.

No mode auto-approves: explicit ask-rule matches, `AskUserQuestion` and MCP tools marked `requiresUserInteraction`, organisation `ask` connector tools, and recognised `rm`/`rmdir` of critical paths (root, top-level dirs, home, the working directory and its parents). In SDK sessions in `auto` mode those removals are denied without calling the callback. Protected paths (`.git`, `.husky`, `.vscode`, most of `.claude`, `.bashrc`, `.npmrc`, `.mcp.json`...) are prompted in default/acceptEdits, denied in dontAsk, and allowed only in bypass.

The `sandbox` option (`SandboxSettings`: `enabled`, `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`, `excludedCommands`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands`, `network`, `filesystem`) confines Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their children at the OS level. Read/Edit/WebFetch, hooks and local MCP servers run outside it. In TypeScript the option merges into an inline `settings.sandbox`: scalars are replaced, restriction lists such as `denyRead` are combined.

`additionalDirectories` / `add_dirs` are passed as `--add-dir`: the directory becomes readable and editable under the same rules, and its skills, commands and subagents load through the `project` setting source; its CLAUDE.md loads only with `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1`, and its hooks and permission rules do not load.
traps: Putting audit or policy checks in `canUseTool`: anything approved by an allow rule, `acceptEdits` or `bypassPermissions` never reaches it. Use a `PreToolUse` hook for checks that must see every call; the SDK warns with `CLAUDE_SDK_CAN_USE_TOOL_SHADOWED` (Python `CanUseToolShadowedWarning`) for bare `allowedTools` entries and bypass mode.

Treating `Bash(curl *)` or `Read(./.env)` deny rules as a security boundary: `/usr/bin/curl`, `sh -c '...'` and a Python script that opens `.env` all slip past. Enforce with the sandbox (`allowedDomains`, `filesystem.denyRead`) or a container.
Writing `Read(/secrets/**)` in `~/.claude/settings.json` and expecting it to protect every project: in user settings `/` anchors at `~/.claude`.
Assuming a more specific allow rule beats a broader deny, or that a hook returning `allow` skips an ask rule. Neither is true.

Expecting an AgentDefinition's `permissionMode: 'plan'` to restrain a subagent when the parent runs in `bypassPermissions`: the subagent inherits bypass. A subagent's own mode applies only when the parent is in `default`, `dontAsk` or `plan`.
Relying on CLAUDE.md or `.claudeignore` to keep secrets away: CLAUDE.md is guidance only and `.claudeignore` has no effect; use Read deny rules.
On Windows with Git Bash, any Bash deny rule silently turns off the PowerShell tool unless `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL=1` or a scoped `PowerShell(...)` rule is set.
